Step 1 · The afocal baseline

plan.contextChunk: This figure shows a two-lens telescope system consisting of a convex objective lens (lens 1, on the left) and a concave eyepiece lens (lens 2, on the right), with the distances f1 and f2 indicated by horizontal brackets beneath the optical axis. Two parallel input rays enter from the left at a small angle δᵢ relative to the optical axis; lens 1 bends them toward the objective focal point to the right of lens 2, and lens 2 then diverges the rays so they exit as a parallel bundle at a larger angle δₒ. The blue vertical marker d shows the offset of the shared focal point from the optical axis in the shown Galilean afocal geometry, where the objective focal point aligns with the eyepiece focal point. This figure demonstrates how a Galilean-style telescope achieves angular magnification equal to the ratio f1/f2 by manipulating ray angles through the two-lens arrangement.

interactionPlan.concept: A Galilean telescope (convex objective + concave eyepiece separated by f₁ − f₂) takes a parallel bundle entering at angle δᵢ and returns a parallel bundle leaving at the larger angle δₒ = (f₁/f₂)·δᵢ, so angular magnification is just the ratio of focal lengths.
elements: Horizontal blue optical axis spanning the full width
Lens 1: tall thin biconvex lens outline (black) on the left, labeled 'lens 1' in blue above it
Lens 2: shorter biconcave lens outline (black) near the right, labeled 'lens 2' in blue above it
Ray A (thick violet): parallel input ray entering above the axis at small angle δᵢ, refracted downward by lens 1, crossing the axis just right of lens 2, exiting below the axis at steeper angle δₒ
Ray B (thin violet): second parallel input ray entering along a lower parallel line at the same angle δᵢ, refracted by lens 1, exiting parallel to ray A after lens 2
Thin blue reference line parallel to the axis at the entry height of each input ray, used to define the angle δᵢ
Curved arrow annotations labeled δᵢ at the left of each input ray (angle between ray and its blue reference line)
Curved arrow annotation labeled δₒ at the right, between the exit ray direction and the optical axis
Dashed violet segment continuing ray B's pre-lens-2 direction to the common focal point
Violet dot marking the common focal point of the two-lens system, below the axis
Small blue dot on the optical axis directly above the focal point, with a short vertical black arrow between them labeled 'd' (the off-axis focal offset)
Horizontal bracket with end ticks under the axis from lens 1 to the focal plane, labeled f₁
Shorter horizontal bracket with end ticks under the axis from lens 2 to the focal plane, labeled f₂
Readout panel showing current f₁, f₂, δᵢ, δₒ and the magnification M = δₒ/δᵢ = f₁/f₂

interactions.teaches: A longer objective focal length pushes the common focal plane farther right and increases angular magnification proportionally.
interactions.label: Objective focal length f₁

interactions.teaches: A shorter (stronger) eyepiece focal length steepens the exit rays and raises the magnification f₁/f₂; the eyepiece must move right to stay afocal.
interactions.label: Eyepiece focal length f₂

interactions.teaches: The output angle scales linearly with the input angle — the ratio δₒ/δᵢ stays fixed while both angles change, and the focal-point offset d = f₁·δᵢ moves off axis.
interactions.label: Input ray angle δᵢ (degrees)

interactions.teaches: Afocal operation is a special alignment condition, not an automatic property of two lenses.
interactions.label: Lock eyepiece to afocal position (f₁ − f₂)

interactions.teaches: Only when the eyepiece sits exactly one f₂ before the objective's focal plane does the bundle exit parallel; moving it makes the exit beam converge or diverge, so the telescope no longer images at infinity.
interactions.label: Eyepiece shift from afocal position (unlock first)

demo_steps.title: The afocal baseline
demo_steps.narration: Two parallel rays arrive tilted by δᵢ. The convex objective aims them at a point one f₁ away, and the concave eyepiece — placed one f₂ short of that point — straightens them into a parallel bundle again, now tilted by the larger angle δₒ.

demo_steps.title: Angle in, angle out
demo_steps.narration: Sweep the input tilt. The focal point slides along the focal plane (d = f₁·δᵢ) and the exit angle follows in lockstep — but the ratio δₒ/δᵢ never budges.

demo_steps.title: Magnification is a ratio
demo_steps.narration: Shorten the eyepiece focal length. The lens separation shrinks to stay afocal, the exit rays fan out much more steeply, and the readout climbs to M = f₁/f₂.

demo_steps.title: Break the afocal condition
demo_steps.narration: Unlock and slide the eyepiece away from f₁ − f₂. The exit bundle is no longer parallel — it converges or diverges — so a distant object no longer appears at infinity to the eye.

demo_steps.title: Restore alignment
demo_steps.narration: Return the eyepiece to the afocal spacing and the bundle snaps back to parallel — this is the focusing adjustment on a real Galilean telescope.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Both lenses share one focal plane, so the off-axis height d = f₁·δᵢ = f₂·δₒ is the same for each — which forces δₒ/δᵢ = f₁/f₂: the telescope's angular magnification is nothing but the ratio of the two focal lengths.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Wide landscape SVG. A thin blue horizontal optical axis runs the full width. Far left third: a tall, narrow black biconvex lens outline labeled 'lens 1' in blue above. About three-quarters across: a shorter black biconcave lens outline labeled 'lens 2' in blue. Two violet rays enter from the left travelling slightly downward at identical small angle δᵢ — one thick (upper, entering well above the axis) and one thin (lower, entering just above the axis); each has a faint blue horizontal reference line at its entry height with a small curved arrow and italic δᵢ label at the far left. Both rays kink at lens 1 toward a common point below the axis a short distance to the right of lens 2, kink again at lens 2, and leave as a parallel pair sloping down-right; a curved arrow labeled δₒ sits at the right margin. A short dashed violet segment shows the thin ray's continuation into the focal point, which is drawn as a filled violet dot. Directly above it on the axis is a small blue dot, joined by a short black vertical arrow labeled 'd'. Beneath the axis: a long bracket with end ticks from lens 1 to the focal plane labeled italic f₁, and a shorter bracket from lens 2 to the focal plane labeled italic f₂. Keep the palette: violet rays, blue axis/labels/reference lines, black lens outlines, brackets and 'd' arrow in black. A small corner readout shows f₁, f₂, δᵢ, δₒ and M = δₒ/δᵢ. When the afocal lock is off and the eyepiece is displaced, the exit rays should visibly converge or diverge instead of running parallel, and the f₂ bracket should no longer terminate at the focal plane.

plan.authoredInteractions:
- Sliders for focal lengths f₁ and f₂: update all ray paths through both lenses and display the angular magnification ratio δₒ/δᵢ = f₁/f₂ in real time, with the lens separation adjusting to maintain the shown Galilean afocal configuration
- Drag the input ray angle δᵢ to change the angle of the two parallel input rays and see the output angle δₒ change proportionally, with ray traces updating through both lenses
- Drag lens 2 along the optical axis to deviate from the shown afocal separation (f₁ - f₂, using the positive bracketed distances), showing the exit beam become converging or diverging and the blue focal-point offset d shift relative to lens 2

authoredContext: A small change in the input ray angle gives a larger change in the output ray angle. The magnification of the telescope is the ratio, $M$, of the angular deviation of an output ray, $\delta_o$, to the angular deviation of an input ray, $\delta_i$.  Writing the focal point offset, $d$, in terms of the rays passing through the centers of lenses 1 and 2 gives the relation, $M = f_1/f_2$, where $f_1$ and $f_2$ are the respective ray focal lengths.

discrepancies: The generated figure adds a white numeric readout panel (f₁/f₂, δi/δo, M, d, afocal check) in the lower-left that has no counterpart in the source; its 11–14px text inside a 1000-unit viewBox renders at roughly 7–8 screen pixels and is effectively unreadable at inline size, and its right edge touches/overlaps the bottom lobe of lens 1.

In the source the thick ray terminates at the shared focal point (purple dot) and only the thin ray continues out to the lower right; in the generated figure the thick ray continues past the focal point to the right edge, so the 'both rays exit parallel' geometry reads differently from the original.

The δₒ arc/arrow is drawn around x≈886 of the viewBox rather than at the far right margin as in the source, so the angle marker sits closer to the exit rays and its label crowds the ray bundle instead of sitting cleanly outside it.
Lens 2's drawn aperture height changes with the ray heights (hh2 is computed from y2), which makes the physical lens appear to grow/shrink as sliders move — the source lens has a fixed aperture.
An orange 'exit rays cross here' circle appears when the eyepiece is un-locked; this is a useful addition but is not in the source figure.
evaluation.notes: A recognizable and well-composed reconstruction of the two-lens afocal (Galilean) ray diagram with correct colors, brackets, δᵢ/δₒ/d annotations and a genuinely useful slider + 5-step demo set; the main weaknesses are an added numeric panel whose text is too small to read and which brushes lens 1, and a few geometric liberties (thick ray extending past the focal point, variable lens-2 aperture).
action_items: Enlarge the readout panel text (≥18 viewBox units, i.e. ~11px on screen) or move it into the HTML UI column, and shift it left/down so it cannot touch lens 1's lower lobe.
Terminate the thick ray at the shared focal point (as in the source) or at least reduce its post-focal extension, and keep both exit rays' geometry visually identical to the original bundle.
Fix lens 2's aperture height to a constant fraction of lens 1's so the drawn lens does not grow/shrink with slider changes; move the δₒ arc to the far right margin like the source.
Qualify the 'd = f₁tanδi = f₂tanδo' readout line so the equality is only asserted while the afocal lock holds (show the two values separately when un-locked).

feedback.rationale: The concept and interaction structure are correct; the issues are concrete implementation fixes (readout text size/placement, ray termination, fixed lens aperture, arc position), and the critic listed no plan-level action items.

discrepancies: Text is scaled small at inline size: 'lens 1'/'lens 2', δᵢ, δₒ, f₁, f₂ and d all render at roughly 10–11 px in the 1000×400 viewBox, whereas in the source these annotations are large and dominant — the label hierarchy the source implies is weakened.

The thin (secondary) ray in the source enters essentially on the axis at lens 1 and its reference line IS the optical axis; the generated version starts it 0.12 units above the axis, so it crosses the axis slightly before lens 1 and sits marginally differently relative to the axis reference line.

The δₒ arc is anchored at a fixed x=900 rather than on the emerging thin ray as in the source, so the arc/arrow floats a little away from the ray it measures and the 'δₒ' glyph sits close to the right margin.
An extra orange crossing-point circle is added (only in the non-afocal state) that has no counterpart in the source figure — acceptable pedagogically but an addition.

In the source the thick ray's leading arrow/hook at the far left is drawn against a separate horizontal blue reference line; the generated reference line is thinner/shorter and the hook arrowhead is smaller, slightly reducing the visual match at the left edge.
evaluation.notes: A faithful and well-constructed reproduction of the Galilean afocal two-lens diagram with correct ray-transfer physics, all key annotations (δᵢ, δₒ, d, f₁, f₂, lens 1/2) and an unusually rich, genuinely pedagogical interaction set; main weaknesses are undersized label text at inline scale and a few small geometric liberties (thin-ray entry height, floating δₒ arc).

feedback.rationale: No failure modes or action items remain and all dimensions score 4–5 with correct concept and interactions; the residual issues are minor cosmetic liberties not worth another iteration.
